soil-env-287.title: Medical geology: when the ground decides who falls ill
soil-env-287.text: Hippocrates and Aristotle were the first to link disease to the elements of the earth. Medical geology is the modern form of that idea: the interdisciplinary science of how natural geological factors affect the health of people and animals. The International Union of Geological Sciences established the field in 1990. It covers exposure to, or deficiency of, trace elements and {{ref:soil-found-029}}, along with mineral dusts, volcanic emissions, radionuclides, microbes and pathogens. Two priorities lead the work. One is the bioavailability of trace elements, the share the body can actually absorb. The other is the baseline background level of harmful natural materials in soil, water, air and food. People who live off the land meet both extremes. In Maputaland, impoverished soils cause diseases of mineral imbalance. In India and Bangladesh, an excess of elements causes toxicity. A shortage of iodine is among the biggest geochemical diseases, partly because humus and clay in soil trap iodine and keep it from people. Other problems are regional. Fluoride troubles Africa and India, and arsenic troubles Argentina, Chile and Taiwan. Selenium is a problem in parts of the US, Venezuela and China, and nitrate in farm areas. Paracelsus summed up the field in one dictum: the dose makes the poison. Its goal is the right balance of element intake.

soil-env-305.title: Chronic wasting disease and the ground that spreads it
soil-env-305.text: For grazing deer, the ground itself may be the main danger. Chronic wasting disease is a fatal transmissible spongiform encephalopathy, a brain-wasting illness caused by prions, in deer, elk, moose and their relatives. Animals catch it by eating grass from soil where infected animals shed prions. The prions stay infectious there for years and bind so tightly to soil particles that the ground may be a major route of transmission. Prions mixed with clay infected deer through the nose. After a Quebec outbreak, inspectors ordered 25 cm of soil decontaminated in parts of the farm.

soil-env-301.title: The hygiene hypothesis and the microbes that may tune immunity
soil-env-301.text: Most mammalian evolution took place in mud and rotting vegetation. The hygiene hypothesis is the idea that early-childhood exposure to certain microorganisms protects against allergies by properly tuning the immune system. In 2003 Graham Rook recast it as the 'old friends' hypothesis, focused on microbes that co-evolved with humans rather than recent crowd infections. It is not about personal cleanliness: poor hygiene raises infection risk without lowering allergy risk. The question is still open. Much evidence supports the hypothesis, yet many scientists reject it, and it struggles to explain allergies in less affluent regions.
